entries.meaning: In a way that shows you don't want to wait. ---
examples: He tapped his foot impatiently while he waited.
The kids are impatiently waiting for summer vacation.
“Come on, hurry up,” she said impatiently.
entries.position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it

entries.meaning: Perfectly, with no faults at all. ---
examples: The waiter was impeccably dressed in a black suit.
The choir performed impeccably last night.
Her manners are impeccably polite.
entries.position: before its word — before participles and adjectives (impeccably dressed); also end

entries.meaning: So slightly or slowly that it can hardly be noticed. ---
examples: The light changed imperceptibly as the sun went down.
She nodded almost imperceptibly.
Prices have been rising slowly, almost imperceptibly, all year.
entries.position: end — after the verb; also mid

entries.meaning: Not completely or not correctly; with faults. ---
examples: The disease is still only imperfectly understood.
I speak Spanish, but imperfectly.
The old photos were imperfectly restored.
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object; before participles

entries.meaning: In a proud, commanding way, expecting to be obeyed. ---
examples: She waved imperiously for the waiter.
“Bring me the file,” he said imperiously.
The cat stared imperiously at its empty bowl.
entries.position: end — usually after a verb of speaking or looking

entries.meaning: Without personal feeling or warmth. ---
examples: The letter was written impersonally, as if by a machine.
Big hospitals can treat patients very impersonally.
He spoke impersonally about the layoffs, never mentioning names.
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object

entries.meaning: Quickly and without thinking first. ---
examples: He impetuously quit his job and moved to Alaska.
She acted impetuously and regretted it later.
The young soldier charged impetuously ahead of the others.
entries.position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it

entries.meaning: In a playful, slightly naughty way. ---
examples: The boy grinned impishly and ran off with the cookie.
She winked impishly at her sister.
“Maybe I did, maybe I didn't,” he said impishly.
entries.position: end — usually after a verb of speaking or looking

entries.meaning: In a way that is hard to believe. ---
examples: The apartment was implausibly cheap for Manhattan.
Implausibly, the hero survives the fall without a scratch.
The team implausibly came back from twenty points down.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives (implausibly cheap); front or mid as a comment

entries.meaning: Implicitly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: By not objecting, he implicitly agreed to the plan.
The contract implicitly allows the data to be shared.
The ad suggests, implicitly, that the car will make you happier.
I trust her implicitly.
The soldiers obeyed their commander implicitly.

senses.head: Without being said directly; understood from what is said or done
examples: By not objecting, he implicitly agreed to the plan.
The contract implicitly allows the data to be shared.
The ad suggests, implicitly, that the car will make you happier.

senses.head: Completely, without any doubt; with trust or believe
examples: I trust her implicitly.
The soldiers obeyed their commander implicitly.

entries.position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it; end after trust, believe
entries.comparison: more/most — in the first sense only
entries.contrast: implicitly is the opposite of explicitly (прямо, открыто), but trust someone implicitly means trust them completely, not trust them indirectly.

entries.meaning: In a way that begs for something. ---
examples: The dog looked up at me imploringly.
“Please don't go,” she said imploringly.
He held out his hands imploringly.
entries.position: end — usually after a verb of speaking or looking

entries.meaning: In a rude way; without good manners. ---
examples: He impolitely interrupted the speaker twice.
I'm sorry if I answered you impolitely.
She kept staring impolitely at his tattoos.
entries.position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it

entries.meaning: Importantly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The car is cheap and, more importantly, safe.
Most importantly, don't forget your passport.
Importantly, the study included both men and women.
He walked importantly up to the podium.
The new manager strutted importantly around the office.

senses.head: Used to point out the most significant fact, usually as more importantly or most importantly
examples: The car is cheap and, more importantly, safe.
Most importantly, don't forget your passport.
Importantly, the study included both men and women.

senses.head: In a self-important way, as if you matter a lot
examples: He walked importantly up to the podium.
The new manager strutted importantly around the office.

entries.type: stance — marking the key point; also manner
entries.position: front — in more importantly, most importantly, with a comma; end in the manner sense
entries.modifies: clauses; verbs in the manner sense

entries.meaning: Extremely; to a degree that seems impossible. ---
examples: The models all looked impossibly thin.
The deadline is impossibly tight.
She stayed impossibly calm during the crisis.
entries.position: before its word

entries.meaning: Not exactly or accurately. ---
examples: The term is often used imprecisely.
The distance was measured imprecisely, so we had to redo it.
He described the location only imprecisely.
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object

entries.meaning: In a way that makes people admire it. ---
examples: The team played impressively in the second half.
The museum's collection is impressively large.
She speaks four languages impressively well.
entries.position: end — after the verb; before its word with adjectives (impressively large)

entries.meaning: In a way that is surprising because it was not likely. ---
examples: Improbably, the smallest team won the championship.
The book is improbably funny for a book about taxes.
The old car improbably made it across the desert.
entries.position: front — with a comma; also mid, and before its word with adjectives

entries.meaning: In a wrong or unacceptable way. ---
examples: The car seat was improperly installed.
Food that is stored improperly can make you sick.
Two officials were accused of acting improperly.
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object; before participles (improperly installed)

entries.meaning: Suddenly, without planning or thinking first. ---
examples: I impulsively bought a plane ticket to Paris.
Don't act impulsively when you're angry.
She shops more impulsively when she's stressed.
entries.position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it

entries.meaning: Very quickly; almost immediately. ---
examples: I'll be back in a flash.
The waiter was at our table in a flash.
In a flash, the thief grabbed her bag and ran.
entries.position: front or end

entries.meaning: In very few words; briefly. ---
examples: In a nutshell, we need more money.
That's the whole story in a nutshell.
So, in a nutshell, the project is two months behind.
entries.position: front or end

entries.meaning: To some extent; in some respects. ---
examples: In a way, I'm glad it happened.
He's right, in a way.
The ending was sad but, in a way, hopeful.
entries.position: any position
entries.contrast: In a way (в каком-то смысле) is not in the way (мешать, загораживать: Your bag is in the way) or on the way (по пути).

entries.meaning: Before a particular time or event. ---
examples: Please buy your tickets in advance.
Thanks in advance for your help.
The landlord asked us to pay a month in advance.
entries.position: end
entries.contrast: Followed by of it becomes a preposition: in advance of the meeting (до встречи).

entries.meaning: In total. ---
examples: In all, more than 500 people attended.
The trip cost about $2,000 in all.
We visited six countries in all.
entries.position: front or end
entries.modifies: a clause with a number or amount
entries.contrast: In all (всего) is not at all (вообще, совсем): There were 30 people in all vs I didn't like it at all.

entries.meaning: Very probably. ---
examples: In all likelihood, the flight will be delayed.
He will, in all likelihood, be the next mayor.
The painting is in all likelihood a fake.
entries.position: any position

entries.meaning: Very probably. ---
examples: In all probability, the storm will miss the coast.
The bill will, in all probability, pass the Senate.
Prices will in all probability keep rising.
entries.position: any position

entries.meaning: Considered alone, without anything else. ---
examples: Money, in and of itself, won't make you happy.
The idea isn't bad in and of itself.
Being late once is not a problem in and of itself.
entries.position: after its word — right after the noun it limits; also end
entries.modifies: a noun or a whole statement

entries.meaning: In any case has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It might rain, but we're going in any case.
In any case, I'll call you when I land.
I can't afford that car, and in any case I don't need one.
I'm not sure what happened. In any case, it's over now.

senses.head: Whatever happens or happened; regardless
examples: It might rain, but we're going in any case.
In any case, I'll call you when I land.

senses.head: Besides; used to add a stronger reason or return to the main point
body: (да и вообще, как бы то ни было)
examples: I can't afford that car, and in any case I don't need one.
I'm not sure what happened. In any case, it's over now.

entries.русский: в любом случае; да и вообще
entries.type: linking — whatever happens; also adds a stronger reason
entries.position: front or end

entries.meaning: Whatever happens or has happened. ---
examples: In any event, the decision is final.
The meeting may be canceled, but we'll send the report in any event.
I don't know if he saw the email; in any event, he didn't reply.
entries.русский: в любом случае, так или иначе
entries.position: front or end

entries.meaning: In a few words; briefly. ---
examples: In brief, the company is doing well.
Here is the news in brief.
The report, in brief, recommends closing two stores.
entries.position: front or end — also mid between commas

entries.meaning: All together, at the same time. ---
examples: 'Good morning!' the children said in chorus.
The fans chanted his name in chorus.
Critics complained in chorus about the new tax.
entries.type: manner — all together at the same time
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Around and around; figuratively, without making any progress. ---
examples: The hawk flew in circles above the field.
We've been going around in circles on this issue for weeks.
He talks in circles and never answers the question.
entries.type: manner — around and around, often getting nowhere
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Deliberately and without feeling or pity. ---
examples: The victims were shot in cold blood.
He murdered his business partner in cold blood.
The soldiers killed the prisoners in cold blood.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Shared by two or more people or things. ---
examples: My sister and I have nothing in common.
What do these three cases have in common?
We had a love of jazz in common.
entries.position: end — after the object of have
entries.modifies: have: have a lot in common
entries.contrast: Russian у нас много общего becomes We have a lot in common, not We have a lot of common. Common alone is an adjective meaning usual (обычный).

entries.meaning: Together, in agreement or cooperation. ---
examples: The two agencies acted in concert to stop the fraud.
Central banks moved in concert to cut interest rates.
The muscles work in concert to move the arm.
entries.position: end
entries.contrast: It can also mean performing live (Springsteen in concert); the adverb means together.

entries.meaning: As a final point; to finish. ---
examples: In conclusion, I'd like to thank our sponsors.
In conclusion, the evidence supports the new policy.
And so, in conclusion, we recommend a second study.
entries.position: front

entries.meaning: Thoroughly, including all the facts. ---
examples: The doctor explained the procedure in detail.
We'll discuss the budget in more detail next week.
She described the attacker in great detail.
entries.type: manner — thoroughly, with all the facts
entries.position: end
entries.contrast: Singular: in detail, not in details. In more detail and in great detail are common.

entries.meaning: At the appropriate time; eventually. ---
examples: You will receive your results in due course.
In due course, the truth came out.
The details will be announced in due course.
entries.type: time — at the proper time, eventually
entries.position: front or end

entries.meaning: Seriously and with full effort; to a real degree. ---
examples: The cleanup began in earnest the next morning.
Once the rain started in earnest, everyone ran inside.
He's been studying in earnest since he failed the first exam.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: In practice, even if not in name. ---
examples: In effect, the new rule bans smoking everywhere downtown.
His silence was, in effect, an admission of guilt.
By cutting the budget, they in effect closed the program.
entries.type: viewpoint — in actual fact, in practice
entries.position: any position
entries.contrast: After be, remain or go into, in effect means in force (в силе, действует): The law is in effect. That use is predicative, not this adverb.

entries.meaning: Basically; in its most important nature. ---
examples: In essence, the two plans are the same.
What he said was, in essence, 'no.'
The job is in essence customer service.
entries.position: any position

entries.meaning: In fact has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Everyone thought she was angry, but in fact she was relieved.
The plant looks dead, but in fact it's just dormant.
I like the city. In fact, I'm thinking of moving there.
It was cold; in fact, it was the coldest day of the year.

senses.head: In reality, contrary to what might be expected
examples: Everyone thought she was angry, but in fact she was relieved.
The plant looks dead, but in fact it's just dormant.

senses.head: Used to add a stronger or more exact point
examples: I like the city. In fact, I'm thinking of moving there.
It was cold; in fact, it was the coldest day of the year.

entries.type: stance — really, actually; also linking: adds a stronger point
entries.position: any position
entries.contrast: False friend: Russian фактически often means practically, virtually, which is in effect or virtually in English. In fact means really or more than that.

entries.meaning: In a position ahead or at the front. ---
examples: Let's sit in front so we can see the screen.
By the tenth mile she was far in front.
The house has a small garden in front.
entries.position: end
entries.contrast: Without of it is an adverb: Let's sit in front. With of it is a preposition: in front of the house. It does not mean напротив (on the other side of a street); that is across from: The bank is across from the hotel.

entries.meaning: Completely; the whole amount or text. ---
examples: The loan must be paid in full by June.
Please write your name in full.
The newspaper printed the letter in full.
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs such as pay, print, write, read

entries.meaning: At the most active or lively stage. ---
examples: By ten o'clock the party was in full swing.
Holiday shopping is in full swing.
When we arrived, the game was already in full swing.
entries.type: time — at the busiest, most active stage
entries.position: end — after be or get

entries.meaning: Usually; considering the whole rather than details. ---
examples: In general, the weather here is mild.
I like his movies in general, but this one was boring.
Americans in general are eating less red meat.
entries.position: front or end — also right after a noun (people in general)
entries.contrast: In general (в целом) is not in common (общего): We have a lot in common. After a noun it means as a whole: teenagers in general.

entries.meaning: Under control; being dealt with. ---
examples: Don't worry, the police have the situation in hand.
Preparations for the wedding are well in hand.
The new coach quickly took the struggling team in hand.
entries.position: end — usually after have, be or take
entries.contrast: Three look-alikes: in hand = under control (The situation is in hand); on hand = available, nearby (под рукой: Keep some cash on hand); at hand = close in time or place (Help is at hand).

entries.meaning: In kind has 2 distinct senses.
examples: When he insulted her, she answered in kind.
The other team played rough, so we responded in kind.
Farmers sometimes paid their rent in kind, with grain.
The company contributed in kind, supplying computers instead of cash.

senses.head: In the same way as one was treated
examples: When he insulted her, she answered in kind.
The other team played rough, so we responded in kind.

senses.head: With goods or services instead of money
examples: Farmers sometimes paid their rent in kind, with grain.
The company contributed in kind, supplying computers instead of cash.

entries.type: manner — in the same way; also in goods rather than money
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs such as respond, reply, pay, donate
entries.contrast: Before a noun it is a hyphenated adjective: in-kind donations. It has nothing to do with kind (добрый).

entries.meaning: In line has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We waited in line for two hours to get tickets.
Please stand in line until your number is called.
The new coach keeps his players in line.
One warning was enough to bring him back in line.

senses.head: In a row of people waiting their turn
examples: We waited in line for two hours to get tickets.
Please stand in line until your number is called.

senses.head: Under control; obeying the rules
examples: The new coach keeps his players in line.
One warning was enough to bring him back in line.

entries.type: place — in a queue; also manner: under control
entries.position: end
entries.contrast: Americans wait in line; the British queue. In line with (в соответствии с) is a preposition: in line with the rules.

entries.meaning: Officially or by title, but not in fact. ---
examples: He's the CEO in name only; his sister actually runs the company.
For their last ten years they were married in name only.
The ceasefire existed in name only.
entries.type: viewpoint — true formally, not in reality
entries.position: after its word — right after the title or noun (a leader in name only)
entries.modifies: a noun or a whole predicate

entries.meaning: Very quickly; almost immediately. ---
examples: Don't worry, we'll be there in no time.
She picked up Spanish in no time.
With four of us helping, the job was done in no time.
entries.type: time — very soon or very quickly
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: a verb or a whole clause

entries.meaning: Because of one's own qualities or position, not because of a connection to someone or something else. ---
examples: Her father was famous, but she's a respected scientist in her own right.
The side dishes are worth the trip in their own right.
Once a small suburb, the town is now a city in its own right.
entries.русский: сам по себе, по собственным заслугам
entries.type: viewpoint — independently, on one's own merits
entries.position: end — the possessive changes with the subject: in her own right, in its own right

entries.meaning: Put another way; that is to say. ---
examples: The flight is overbooked. In other words, some of us won't get on.
He said he'd think about it — in other words, no.
So, in other words, you forgot.
entries.type: linking — restating something more simply or plainly
entries.position: front or end

entries.meaning: Especially; more than the others. ---
examples: I loved the whole menu, but the desserts in particular were amazing.
Is there anything in particular you'd like to see?
Crime has fallen across the city, car thefts in particular.
entries.type: focusing — singling out one item from a group
entries.position: after its word — right after the noun it picks out (one student in particular), or at the end
entries.modifies: a noun phrase or a whole clause
entries.contrast: Particularly goes before its word (particularly good); in particular follows it (this one in particular). Nothing in particular = ничего особенного.

entries.meaning: Briefly, while talking or writing about something else. ---
examples: She mentioned in passing that she'd quit her job.
The book refers to the war only in passing.
I met him once, in passing, at a conference.
entries.type: manner — briefly, as a side remark
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Physically present, not by phone, mail or online. ---
examples: You have to apply in person at the DMV.
She looks taller in person than on TV.
We've emailed for years but never met in person.
entries.type: manner — physically present, face to face
entries.position: end
entries.contrast: Russian лично covers two English words. In person means physically present: I spoke to her in person (face to face). Personally gives an opinion: Personally, I think it's a mistake (лично я считаю).

entries.meaning: In place has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Hold the shelf in place while I drill.
A few bobby pins kept her hat in place.
The coach had us jog in place to warm up.
The new security rules are already in place.
We need a plan in place before hurricane season.

senses.head: In the right or usual position; not moving
examples: Hold the shelf in place while I drill.
A few bobby pins kept her hat in place.
The coach had us jog in place to warm up.

senses.head: Set up and working; in effect
examples: The new security rules are already in place.
We need a plan in place before hurricane season.

entries.type: place — in position; also a state of being set up
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs such as hold, stay, put, keep, and be
entries.contrast: In place of is a preposition meaning instead of (вместо): She went in place of her boss. Out of place = неуместный. Americans run in place; British English says run on the spot.

entries.meaning: In what really happens, as opposed to what should happen. ---
examples: The law sounds fair, but in practice it's rarely enforced.
In practice, most customers never read the terms.
It works on paper; in practice, not so much.
entries.type: viewpoint — what actually happens, as opposed to theory
entries.position: front or end
entries.contrast: Out of practice means no longer skilled because of lack of training (потерял навык).

entries.meaning: As a general idea, though the details or practice may be different. ---
examples: The board has agreed in principle, but the details still need work.
In principle, anyone can apply; in reality, few are accepted.
I'm not against the idea in principle.
entries.type: viewpoint — in general terms, before the details
entries.position: front or end
entries.modifies: a verb or a whole clause
entries.contrast: A false friend. Russian в принципе often means basically or generally speaking (В принципе, я свободен = Basically, I'm free). English in principle means as an idea, though not yet in practice or in detail: They agreed in principle = they accepted the idea, details still to come. Don't confuse principle with principal.

entries.meaning: Without other people watching or listening. ---
examples: Can I talk to you in private for a minute?
The committee met in private before the vote.
Praise people in public and criticize them in private.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Where other people can see or hear. ---
examples: He hates speaking in public.
She hasn't been seen in public since the scandal.
Please don't argue with me in public.
entries.type: manner — where other people can see or hear
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Actually, as opposed to how something seems or was expected to be. ---
examples: The job sounded glamorous; in reality, it was mostly paperwork.
In reality, few people read the fine print.
They seem rich, but in reality they're deep in debt.
entries.type: viewpoint — contrasting how things seem with how they are
entries.position: front or end

entries.meaning: As a way of paying back or answering something someone did. ---
examples: I helped him move, and in return he fixed my car.
What do you want in return?
She smiled, and he smiled in return.
entries.type: manner — as an exchange or a response
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: a verb or a whole clause
entries.contrast: With a noun it becomes in return for: in return for your help. Don't confuse with in turn (по очереди; в свою очередь).

entries.meaning: Without other people knowing. ---
examples: The two companies had been negotiating in secret for months.
They got married in secret in Las Vegas.
He practiced the speech in secret so no one would laugh.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: To sum up in a few words. ---
examples: The hotel was dirty, loud and overpriced. In short, avoid it.
In short, we need more money.
He's smart, reliable and kind — in short, the perfect hire.
entries.position: front
entries.contrast: Not the same as shortly, which means soon (скоро). In casual speech Americans also say long story short.

entries.meaning: Quickly; without delay. ---
examples: The police arrived in short order.
The new owners replaced the entire staff in short order.
Once the parts came in, the mechanic had the car fixed in short order.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: In large amounts; to a very high degree. ---
examples: She has talent in spades.
He paid me back in spades.
The movie promised action, and it delivered in spades.
entries.type: degree — to a very great extent; informal
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: a verb or a noun it follows (talent in spades)

entries.meaning: Calmly, without letting a problem upset or stop you. ---
examples: She took the bad news in stride.
Rookies often panic under pressure, but he takes it all in stride.
The kids took the move to a new city in stride.
entries.position: end — almost always in take something in stride
entries.contrast: American usage; British English says take something in one's stride.

entries.meaning: Together, or at the same time as something else. ---
examples: The two departments work in tandem on product launches.
Prices and wages rose in tandem.
The drug works best in tandem with physical therapy.
entries.type: manner — together, at the same time
entries.position: end — often in tandem with + noun

entries.meaning: At first; at the start, before things changed. ---
examples: In the beginning, I hated living in the city.
It was hard in the beginning, but it gets easier.
In the beginning we had no customers at all.
entries.type: time — at first, in contrast to later
entries.position: front or end
entries.contrast: Russian в начале covers two English phrases. In the beginning = at first, before things changed (поначалу). At the beginning of + noun marks the start of something named: at the beginning of the movie, not in the beginning of the movie. The same split applies to in the end / at the end of.

entries.meaning: Finally, after a long process or a lot of discussion. ---
examples: We argued for an hour, but in the end we ordered pizza.
In the end, it's your decision.
It was a tough season, but they won the title in the end.
entries.type: time — finally, after everything; also linking
entries.position: front or end
entries.contrast: In the end = finally, after a process (в итоге). At the end (of) = at the last point of something: at the end of the street, at the end of the movie. In the end of the movie is a common mistake.

entries.meaning: In the first place has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Why did you agree to it in the first place?
If you hadn't lied in the first place, we wouldn't be in this mess.
I never wanted to come in the first place.
In the first place, we can't afford it; in the second place, we don't need it.
In the first place, the report is late.

senses.head: At the very beginning; at all — usually when asking or complaining about why something happened
examples: Why did you agree to it in the first place?
If you hadn't lied in the first place, we wouldn't be in this mess.
I never wanted to come in the first place.

senses.head: First of all, as the first in a list of reasons
examples: In the first place, we can't afford it; in the second place, we don't need it.
In the first place, the report is late.

entries.type: time — originally, to begin with; also linking
entries.position: end — for originally; front when listing reasons
entries.contrast: The end-position use (Why did you go there in the first place?) is far more common than the list use, and Russian во-первых does not cover it; think вообще or с самого начала.

entries.meaning: At all; even slightly — after not or another negative. ---
examples: I'm not in the least worried.
“Did the delay bother you?” “Not in the least.”
She didn't seem in the least surprised.
entries.position: before its word — or end (Not in the least)
entries.modifies: an adjective, a verb, or a whole negative clause

entries.meaning: Over a long period of time; eventually. ---
examples: Buying good boots saves money in the long run.
In the long run, the new highway will ease traffic.
It's painful now, but it'll be better for everyone in the long run.
entries.русский: в конечном счёте, в долгосрочной перспективе
entries.type: time — over a long period, eventually
entries.position: front or end
entries.contrast: The opposite is in the short run or in the short term.

entries.meaning: In a difficult situation without the help someone was counting on. ---
examples: Our babysitter canceled at the last minute and left us in the lurch.
The contractor quit halfway through, leaving the owners in the lurch.
I won't leave you in the lurch — I'll finish before I go.
entries.type: manner — without help when help is needed
entries.position: end — almost always in leave someone in the lurch

entries.meaning: During the time before something expected happens. ---
examples: The doctor will see you soon. In the meantime, please fill out this form.
Our new place isn't ready, so we're staying with friends in the meantime.
In the meantime, keep an eye on the weather.
entries.type: time — during the period until something happens
entries.position: front or end

entries.meaning: At the last possible moment; just before it is too late. ---
examples: The firefighters arrived in the nick of time.
I made the train in the nick of time.
She hit the brakes in the nick of time.
entries.русский: в последний момент, как раз вовремя
entries.type: time — just before it is too late
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: At the same moment — used when two statements contradict each other, or when two things are wrongly treated as equal. ---
examples: He said he trusted me and, in the same breath, asked to see my receipts.
You can't praise the plan and criticize it in the same breath.
His name shouldn't be mentioned in the same breath as the great players.
entries.type: time — at the same moment, usually of contradictory statements
entries.position: mid or end

entries.meaning: According to what should happen, though reality may be different. ---
examples: In theory, the train takes two hours.
It sounds great in theory, but will it work?
In theory, anyone can become president.
entries.type: viewpoint — how things should work, as opposed to practice
entries.position: front or end

entries.meaning: In time has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We got to the airport in time for our flight.
Will the package arrive in time for Christmas?
The ambulance got there just in time.
In time, you'll forget all about him.
The pain will fade in time.

senses.head: Early enough; before it is too late
examples: We got to the airport in time for our flight.
Will the package arrive in time for Christmas?
The ambulance got there just in time.

senses.head: Eventually; after enough time has passed
examples: In time, you'll forget all about him.
The pain will fade in time.

entries.position: end — front is common for eventually
entries.modifies: a verb or a whole clause; often in time for + noun or in time to + verb
entries.contrast: Russian вовремя covers two English phrases. On time = at the scheduled moment, not late: The train left on time. In time = early enough for something: We arrived in time to get seats.

entries.meaning: Really; as is actually the case. ---
examples: He said he was fine, but in truth he was terrified.
In truth, I never liked the place.
The deal was, in truth, a disaster.
entries.русский: по правде говоря, на самом деле
entries.type: stance — admitting what is really true
entries.position: front — or mid between commas
entries.contrast: Somewhat formal and written; in speech Americans say to tell the truth, honestly or actually.

entries.meaning: In turn has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Higher gas prices raise shipping costs, which in turn raise food prices.
She trained the managers, who in turn trained their teams.
He was kind to me, and I, in turn, tried to help others.
The students spoke in turn about their projects.
She looked at each of us in turn.

senses.head: As a result of that, in a chain of causes and effects
examples: Higher gas prices raise shipping costs, which in turn raise food prices.
She trained the managers, who in turn trained their teams.
He was kind to me, and I, in turn, tried to help others.

senses.head: One after another, in order
examples: The students spoke in turn about their projects.
She looked at each of us in turn.

entries.position: mid or end
entries.modifies: a verb or a whole clause
entries.contrast: Take turns is the usual way to say делать по очереди: We took turns driving. Don't confuse in turn with in return (взамен).

entries.meaning: In unison has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The class answered in unison.
The dancers moved in unison.
“Happy birthday!” they shouted in unison.
The allies acted in unison against the threat.
Both parties voted in unison for the bill.

senses.head: At the same moment, saying or doing the same thing
examples: The class answered in unison.
The dancers moved in unison.
“Happy birthday!” they shouted in unison.

senses.head: In complete agreement
examples: The allies acted in unison against the threat.
Both parties voted in unison for the bill.

entries.type: manner — together, at the same time
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Without success; with no result. ---
examples: We searched in vain for the keys.
The doctors tried in vain to save him.
All our hard work was in vain.
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: a verb; also after be (it was all in vain)
entries.contrast: The adjective vain means conceited (тщеславный); in vain is only about wasted effort. Take someone's name in vain = speak of them disrespectfully.

entries.meaning: Written down, especially as an official record. ---
examples: Can you give me that offer in writing?
All complaints must be submitted in writing.
Get the landlord's promise in writing.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Not correctly or exactly. ---
examples: The article inaccurately reported the number of victims.
His name was spelled inaccurately on the list.
The old map shows the border inaccurately.
entries.position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it

entries.meaning: Not well enough, or not enough. ---
examples: Many of the new workers were inadequately trained.
The house was inadequately heated in winter.
The problem has been addressed inadequately so far.
entries.position: before its word — before participles (inadequately trained); also end

entries.meaning: By accident, without meaning to. ---
examples: I inadvertently deleted the whole file.
He inadvertently left the back door unlocked.
The email was sent inadvertently to the entire company.
entries.position: mid — before the main verb; also end

entries.meaning: In a silly, pointless way. ---
examples: He grinned inanely at the camera.
They chatted inanely about the weather for an hour.
The host laughed inanely at his own jokes.
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object

entries.meaning: In a way that is not suitable or acceptable. ---
examples: He was fired for behaving inappropriately with clients.
She was inappropriately dressed for a funeral.
The teacher laughed inappropriately at the student's mistake.
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object; before participles (inappropriately dressed)

entries.meaning: Too quietly to be heard. ---
examples: He muttered something inaudibly and left.
She whispered inaudibly to her friend.
The engine was running almost inaudibly.
entries.position: end — usually after a verb of speaking or looking

entries.meaning: In a way that suggests things will not go well. ---
examples: The season began inauspiciously with three straight losses.
Their marriage started inauspiciously, in a snowstorm that closed the roads.
The new restaurant opened inauspiciously on the day of a blackout.
entries.position: end — usually after begin, start, open

entries.meaning: Without stopping, again and again. ---
examples: The neighbor's dog barked incessantly all night.
It rained incessantly for a week.
He talks incessantly about his new car.
entries.type: manner — without stopping, usually of something annoying
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object

entries.meaning: In a clear, sharp way that goes straight to the point. ---
examples: She writes incisively about politics.
The report incisively identifies the company's weaknesses.
He argued more incisively than any other lawyer in the room.
entries.position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it

entries.meaning: Hiding who you really are, especially when you are famous. ---
examples: The singer traveled incognito in a baseball cap and sunglasses.
The CEO went incognito to see how the stores were really run.
The prince spent a week in New York incognito.
entries.position: end — after travel, go, stay
entries.form: borrowed from Italian; the same form is an adjective
entries.contrast: Also an adjective with the same meaning (The star was incognito); incognito mode in a web browser is the adjective.

entries.meaning: In a confused way that is hard to understand. ---
examples: The man was mumbling incoherently when the police arrived.
She was so upset that she spoke incoherently.
The report was written incoherently, jumping from topic to topic.
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object

entries.meaning: Far more than anything else; beyond comparison. ---
examples: The new phone is incomparably faster than the old one.
She was an incomparably gifted pianist.
Life in the city is incomparably more expensive.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives and comparatives (incomparably better)

entries.meaning: Without the skill or ability to do something well. ---
examples: The project was managed incompetently from the start.
The repairs were done so incompetently that we had to redo them.
Critics say the city handled the snowstorm incompetently.
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object

entries.meaning: Not fully; with parts missing. ---
examples: The process is still incompletely understood.
The form was filled out incompletely, so it was rejected.
The old wound had healed only incompletely.
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object; before participles (incompletely understood)

entries.meaning: To a degree that is almost impossible to imagine. ---
examples: The universe is inconceivably large.
The price was inconceivably high for a used car.
Ten years ago, this technology would have seemed inconceivably advanced.
entries.position: before its word

entries.meaning: Without a clear result or decision. ---
examples: The peace talks ended inconclusively late last night.
The investigation closed inconclusively, with no one charged.
The debate ended inconclusively, with neither side giving ground.
entries.position: end — usually after end, close, finish

entries.meaning: In a way that seems strange or out of place. ---
examples: A pink plastic flamingo stood incongruously in the snowy yard.
The music was incongruously cheerful for such a sad movie.
He was dressed incongruously in a tuxedo at the barbecue.
entries.position: end — after the verb; also before its word (incongruously cheerful)

entries.meaning: Not in the same way every time. ---
examples: The rules are enforced inconsistently from school to school.
The team has played inconsistently all season.
The word is spelled inconsistently throughout the report.
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object

entries.meaning: Without attracting attention. ---
examples: I slipped out of the meeting as inconspicuously as possible.
The camera was mounted inconspicuously above the door.
The detective sat inconspicuously in the corner of the diner.
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object

entries.meaning: In a way that causes trouble or comes at a bad time. ---
examples: The only pharmacy is inconveniently located on the other side of town.
The meeting was inconveniently scheduled for 7 a.m.
Inconveniently, my phone died just as the taxi arrived.
entries.position: before its word — before participles (inconveniently located); also end, or front with a comma

entries.meaning: In a way that is wrong or not true. ---
examples: You answered the last question incorrectly.
The box was incorrectly labeled as fragile.
Many people pronounce the word incorrectly.
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object; before participles (incorrectly labeled)

entries.meaning: More and more, over time. ---
examples: It's becoming increasingly difficult to find a cheap apartment.
Increasingly, people are choosing to work from home.
She grew increasingly worried as the hours passed.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives (increasingly difficult); mid before verbs; front with a comma
entries.contrast: increasingly already means 'more and more', so increasingly more difficult is redundant: say increasingly difficult or more and more difficult (всё труднее).

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you cannot believe something. ---
examples: “You won the lottery?” she asked incredulously.
He stared incredulously at the bill.
The crowd watched incredulously as the underdog took the lead.
entries.position: end — usually after a verb of speaking or looking
entries.contrast: incredulously = not believing (недоверчиво); incredibly = unbelievably, very (невероятно).

entries.meaning: In a way that cannot be cured or changed. ---
examples: By the time the doctors found the tumor, he was incurably ill.
She's an incurably romantic person.
My father is incurably optimistic about his baseball team.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives (incurably ill, incurably romantic)

entries.meaning: In a shocking or improper way; more than is acceptable. ---
examples: He was arrested for exposing himself indecently in the park.
Her skirt was indecently short for a job interview.
We left the party indecently early.
entries.position: end — after the verb; before its word with adjectives (indecently early)

entries.meaning: Unable to decide; in a hesitant way. ---
examples: She hovered indecisively between the two dresses.
The mayor has acted indecisively throughout the crisis.
He stood indecisively at the door, not sure whether to knock.
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object

entries.meaning: Permanently, in a way that cannot be removed or forgotten. ---
examples: That summer is indelibly printed on my memory.
The war marked his generation indelibly.
The name was written indelibly on the label with a marker.
entries.position: before its word — before participles (indelibly printed); also end

entries.meaning: Independently has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The kids learned to work independently at a young age.
She lives independently despite her disability.
The investigation will be run independently of the police department.
Two scientists discovered the same process independently.
Each witness was interviewed independently.

senses.head: On your own, without help or control from others
examples: The kids learned to work independently at a young age.
She lives independently despite her disability.
The investigation will be run independently of the police department.

senses.head: Separately, without any contact or influence between the people or things involved
examples: Two scientists discovered the same process independently.
Each witness was interviewed independently.

entries.position: end — after the verb and its object; independently of before a noun
entries.contrast: Russian независимо от is usually regardless of: regardless of the weather, not independently of the weather. Independently of (not from) means separately from: The two systems work independently of each other.

entries.meaning: To a degree too great to describe. ---
examples: The view from the top was indescribably beautiful.
The smell in the room was indescribably bad.
I felt indescribably happy when I saw her again.
entries.position: before its word

entries.meaning: Without interest or concern. ---
examples: He shrugged indifferently when I told him the news.
The clerk glanced indifferently at my ticket and waved me through.
The staff treated our complaints indifferently.
entries.position: end — usually after a verb of speaking or looking

entries.meaning: In an angry way, because something seems unfair. ---
examples: “I did not take your pen!” he said indignantly.
She indignantly denied the rumor.
Customers complained indignantly about the price increase.
entries.position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it

entries.meaning: Not directly; through another person, thing or step. ---
examples: The new law will affect everyone, directly or indirectly.
She hinted indirectly that she wanted to leave.
The fire was indirectly caused by the heat wave.
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object; before participles (indirectly caused)

entries.meaning: Carelessly, saying or showing things that should stay private. ---
examples: He indiscreetly mentioned the surprise party in front of her.
The details of the deal were indiscreetly leaked to the press.
She talked indiscreetly about her boss at the bar.
entries.position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it
entries.contrast: indiscreetly = without keeping secrets (неосторожно, болтливо); indiscriminately = without choosing (без разбора).

entries.meaning: Without choosing carefully; at random. ---
examples: The gunman fired indiscriminately into the crowd.
Antibiotics should not be used indiscriminately.
He reads indiscriminately, from comic books to philosophy.
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object

entries.meaning: Not clearly enough to be seen, heard or remembered well. ---
examples: He spoke so indistinctly that nobody understood him.
Through the fog we could see the lighthouse only indistinctly.
Voices murmured indistinctly behind the wall.
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object

entries.meaning: Separately, one at a time. ---
examples: The candies are individually wrapped.
The teacher met with each student individually.
Individually, the players are good, but they don't work well as a team.
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object; before participles (individually wrapped); front with a comma

entries.meaning: In a kind, tolerant way, letting someone have what they want. ---
examples: Grandma smiled indulgently as the kids ate their third dessert.
The teacher listened indulgently to his long excuse.
Her parents treated her indulgently and rarely said no.
entries.position: end — usually after a verb of speaking or looking
entries.contrast: Russian снисходительно has two English matches: indulgently is warm and tolerant; condescendingly is the negative one, looking down on someone.

entries.meaning: In a hard-working, busy way. ---
examples: The students worked industriously on their projects.
Ants moved industriously back and forth across the path.
She typed away industriously all afternoon.
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object
entries.contrast: industriously is about working hard (усердно), not about industry; 'by industry' is industrially.

entries.meaning: Without producing the result you want. ---
examples: The problem has been handled ineffectively for years.
He tried ineffectively to calm the angry crowd.
Money that is spent ineffectively doesn't help anyone.
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object

entries.meaning: In a weak way that fails to achieve anything. ---
examples: She waved her arms ineffectually at the swarm of bees.
The police tried ineffectually to stop the protest.
He pushed ineffectually against the heavy door.
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object

entries.meaning: In a way that wastes time, money or energy. ---
examples: Old buildings use energy very inefficiently.
The office is run inefficiently, with far too many meetings.
The factory was operating inefficiently before the upgrade.
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object
entries.contrast: Russian неэффективно covers two words: ineffectively = without getting the result; inefficiently = wasting time, money or energy along the way.

entries.meaning: Without skill; clumsily. ---
examples: The new manager handled the crisis ineptly.
He ineptly tried to fix the sink and flooded the kitchen.
The movie is ineptly edited and hard to follow.
entries.position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it

entries.meaning: In a way that cannot be avoided or denied. ---
examples: The conclusion is inescapably clear: we need more money.
Inescapably, the costs will be passed on to customers.
Her life is inescapably tied to the town where she grew up.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives and participles (inescapably clear); also front

entries.meaning: As was certain to happen; unavoidably. ---
examples: Inevitably, the project cost more than planned.
Prices will inevitably go up next year.
Whenever we talk politics, it inevitably ends in an argument.
entries.position: front — with a comma; also mid, before the main verb

entries.meaning: In a way that is too bad to be forgiven. ---
examples: The train was inexcusably late again.
He behaved inexcusably toward his sister.
The report was inexcusably careless with the numbers.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives (inexcusably late); also end

entries.meaning: In a way that cannot be stopped or changed. ---
examples: Prices have risen slowly but inexorably.
The river is inexorably eating away at the cliff.
The country moved inexorably toward war.
entries.position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it

entries.meaning: Without costing much money. ---
examples: You can furnish an apartment inexpensively with used furniture.
The hotel is inexpensively priced but very clean.
We ate inexpensively at food trucks during the trip.
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object; before participles (inexpensively priced)

entries.meaning: So closely that the things cannot be separated. ---
examples: Poverty and poor health are inextricably linked.
His name is inextricably tied to the company he founded.
The two stories are inextricably bound together.
entries.position: before its word — before participles (inextricably linked)

entries.meaning: In a way that quickly spreads the feeling to other people. ---
examples: She laughed infectiously, and soon the whole room was laughing.
The song is infectiously catchy.
He's infectiously enthusiastic about everything he does.
entries.position: end — after laugh, smile; before its word with adjectives (infectiously cheerful)

entries.meaning: Infinitely has 2 distinct senses.
examples: This version is infinitely better than the first one.
I'd infinitely prefer to stay home tonight.
In theory, the line can be extended infinitely in both directions.
The pattern on the screen seemed to repeat infinitely.

senses.head: Very much; far, usually before a comparative
examples: This version is infinitely better than the first one.
I'd infinitely prefer to stay home tonight.

senses.head: Without any limit or end
examples: In theory, the line can be extended infinitely in both directions.
The pattern on the screen seemed to repeat infinitely.

entries.position: before its word — before comparatives and adjectives (infinitely better)

entries.meaning: In a way that refuses to change or adapt. ---
examples: The rules were applied inflexibly, with no exceptions for anyone.
He stuck inflexibly to his original plan.
Some managers react inflexibly when staff ask to work from home.
entries.position: end — or before an adjective (inflexibly strict)

entries.meaning: In a relaxed, casual or unofficial way. ---
examples: We met informally over coffee before the interview.
The committee is informally known as the Friday group.
Most people dress more informally at work than they used to.
entries.position: end — also mid before a participle (informally known as)

entries.meaning: Not often. ---
examples: The buses run infrequently on Sundays.
We see each other only infrequently now that she lives in Denver.
Not infrequently, the simplest answer is the right one.
entries.position: mid or end
entries.contrast: Not infrequently is a common formal way to say 'fairly often'.

entries.meaning: In a clever, original and inventive way. ---
examples: The tiny apartment was ingeniously designed to feel bigger.
She ingeniously used a paper clip to fix the zipper.
The plot is ingeniously constructed, with a twist in every chapter.
entries.position: mid or end — also before a participle or adjective (ingeniously designed)
entries.contrast: Do not confuse with ingenuously 'naively, openly' — one letter apart and a different meaning.

entries.meaning: In a way meant to win someone's favor, often insincerely. ---
examples: The salesman smiled ingratiatingly and offered us coffee.
He laughed ingratiatingly at all of his boss's jokes.
"Anything else I can do for you?" she asked ingratiatingly.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Because of the basic nature of something, not because of outside factors. ---
examples: Rock climbing is inherently dangerous.
There's nothing inherently wrong with borrowing money.
Some jobs are inherently stressful, no matter who does them.
entries.type: degree — 'by its very nature', before an adjective
entries.position: before its word — usually an adjective (inherently risky)
entries.modifies: adjectives, and verbs (it inherently involves risk)

entries.meaning: In a cruel way that causes needless suffering. ---
examples: The animals were kept inhumanely in tiny cages.
Prisoners said they had been treated inhumanely.
The report found that the workers were housed inhumanely.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: As part of someone's nature from birth, not learned. ---
examples: Children are innately curious about the world.
Do you think people are innately good?
Some of us are just innately better at math.
entries.type: degree — 'from birth, by nature', before an adjective
entries.position: before its word — usually an adjective (innately curious)

entries.meaning: Without meaning any harm, or in a way that pretends to know nothing. ---
examples: "Who, me?" he asked innocently.
It all started innocently enough, with a joke at dinner.
She innocently mentioned the party, not knowing he wasn't invited.
entries.position: end — also mid (she innocently asked)

entries.meaning: To an unusually or unreasonably large degree. ---
examples: He was inordinately proud of his lawn.
The meeting took an inordinately long time.
She seemed inordinately pleased with such a small gift.
entries.type: degree — an intensifier meaning 'more than is reasonable'
entries.position: before its word

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you want to know something. ---
examples: She looked at me inquiringly, waiting for an explanation.
The dog tilted its head inquiringly.
He raised his eyebrows inquiringly but said nothing.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: With eager curiosity, wanting to find things out. ---
examples: The kids peered inquisitively into the box.
A squirrel watched us inquisitively from a branch.
"What's in the bag?" she asked inquisitively.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Insanely has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The tacos at that place are insanely good.
Rent in San Francisco is insanely expensive.
She's been insanely busy since she started the new job.
He laughed insanely, like a villain in a cartoon.
The crowd screamed insanely when the band came on.

senses.head: Extremely; used informally for emphasis
examples: The tacos at that place are insanely good.
Rent in San Francisco is insanely expensive.
She's been insanely busy since she started the new job.

senses.head: In a crazy, wild or reckless way
examples: He laughed insanely, like a villain in a cartoon.
The crowd screamed insanely when the band came on.

entries.position: before its word — for 'extremely'; end in the manner sense (behaved insanely)
entries.modifies: adjectives and adverbs; verbs in the manner sense

entries.meaning: In a way that can never be satisfied. ---
examples: My daughter is insatiably curious about space.
He read insatiably, a book every couple of days.
The company seemed insatiably hungry for growth.
entries.type: degree — before an adjective; also manner
entries.position: before its word — usually curious or hungry; end after a verb

entries.meaning: Not firmly fixed or not safely protected. ---
examples: The ladder was insecurely propped against the wall.
Millions of passwords had been stored insecurely.
The load was tied down insecurely and fell off the truck.
entries.position: end — also before a participle (insecurely fastened)

entries.meaning: Without thinking about other people's feelings. ---
examples: The news was handled very insensitively.
He joked insensitively about her illness.
I'm sorry if I spoke insensitively yesterday.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: In a way that cannot be separated. ---
examples: Health and income are inseparably linked.
In most people's minds, the two ideas are inseparably tied.
Her name is inseparably connected with the civil rights movement.
entries.position: before its word — usually a participle (inseparably linked)

entries.meaning: Inside out has 2 distinct senses.
examples: You've got your sweater on inside out.
Turn the jeans inside out before you wash them.
The wind blew my umbrella inside out.
She knows the tax code inside out.
After ten years there, he knew the building inside out.

senses.head: With the inner side turned to the outside
examples: You've got your sweater on inside out.
Turn the jeans inside out before you wash them.
The wind blew my umbrella inside out.

senses.head: Thoroughly, in every detail
examples: She knows the tax code inside out.
After ten years there, he knew the building inside out.

entries.position: end
entries.contrast: Inside out = наизнанку; upside down = вверх ногами; backwards (British back to front) = задом наперёд.

entries.meaning: Gradually and quietly, in a harmful way that is hard to notice. ---
examples: The disease develops insidiously, with no early symptoms.
Doubt crept insidiously into his mind.
Stereotypes insidiously shape how we judge people.
entries.position: mid or end

entries.meaning: Without really meaning what you say or show. ---
examples: She smiled insincerely and said she loved the gift.
He apologized, but rather insincerely.
Politicians who speak insincerely are easy to spot.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: In a firm, repeated way that will not accept no. ---
examples: The phone rang insistently until I picked it up.
The cat meowed insistently at the door.
"You have to come," she said insistently.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: In a rude, disrespectful way. ---
examples: The boy stared insolently at the teacher.
He answered insolently and was sent to the principal's office.
She shrugged insolently and walked away.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Immediately, with no delay at all. ---
examples: The message arrives almost instantaneously.
The driver was killed instantaneously.
The lights came on instantaneously when we opened the door.
entries.position: end — also mid

entries.meaning: Without thinking, because of a natural reaction or feeling. ---
examples: I instinctively ducked when the ball flew toward me.
Instinctively, she knew something was wrong.
Babies turn instinctively toward their mother's voice.
entries.position: mid — also front or end

entries.meaning: In a way that concerns an organization or system rather than individuals. ---
examples: The report called the department institutionally biased.
The college is institutionally committed to free speech.
Discrimination can be institutionally built into hiring rules.
entries.type: viewpoint — in terms of organizations and their systems
entries.position: before its word — usually an adjective (institutionally racist)

entries.meaning: Not enough; less than is needed. ---
examples: The chicken was insufficiently cooked.
Many new teachers feel insufficiently prepared.
The building was insufficiently insulated for Chicago winters.
entries.position: before its word

entries.meaning: In an offensive way, or so much that it feels offensive. ---
examples: They made us an insultingly low offer for the house.
The questions on the test were insultingly easy.
He spoke to the waiter insultingly.
entries.type: degree — before an adjective; also manner
entries.position: before its word — for 'offensively' (insultingly low); end in the manner sense

entries.meaning: As an essential part of something, in a way that cannot be separated from the whole. ---
examples: She was integrally involved in planning the project.
Jazz is integrally connected to the history of New Orleans.
The flash is integrally built into the camera body.
entries.position: before its word — usually a participle (integrally involved)

entries.meaning: In a way that concerns the mind, thinking or ideas. ---
examples: The course is intellectually demanding.
Intellectually, I know he's right, but it still feels unfair.
Kids need to be challenged intellectually.
entries.type: viewpoint — in terms of the mind and thinking
entries.position: any position — before an adjective (intellectually honest); front with a comma; end after a verb

entries.meaning: In a smart, well-thought-out way. ---
examples: She spoke intelligently about the risks.
Use your budget intelligently.
The museum is intelligently laid out, so you never get lost.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Clearly enough to be understood. ---
examples: He was so upset he could barely speak intelligibly.
Try to write intelligibly so the grader can follow your argument.
The robot can answer questions fairly intelligibly.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Very strongly; with great feeling or to a great degree. ---
examples: He's an intensely private person.
She stared at the screen intensely.
I disliked the book intensely.
entries.type: degree — before an adjective; also manner
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective (intensely private); end after a verb
entries.contrast: Intensely means 'with strong feeling or to a great degree' (intensely private); intensively means 'with a lot of concentrated effort' (trained intensively). Russian интенсивно usually matches intensively.

entries.meaning: With a lot of effort or activity in a short time or small area. ---
examples: The team trained intensively for the final.
She studied Spanish intensively for three months.
This land has been farmed intensively for decades.
entries.position: end — also before a participle (intensively farmed)
entries.contrast: Not the same as intensely: intensively is about concentrated effort or use (study intensively), intensely about strength of feeling (intensely jealous).

entries.meaning: On purpose; deliberately. ---
examples: I didn't hurt your feelings intentionally.
The fire was set intentionally.
He intentionally left the door open for the cat.
entries.position: mid or end

entries.meaning: With close, fixed attention. ---
examples: The kids listened intently to the story.
He was watching her intently.
She leaned forward and studied the map intently.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: In a way that lets one thing be used in place of another. ---
examples: People often use affect and effect interchangeably, but they're different.
The two cables can be used interchangeably.
In this article, app and program are used interchangeably.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: For so long that it seems it will never end; tediously long. ---
examples: The meeting dragged on interminably.
We waited interminably at the DMV.
His speech was interminably long.
entries.position: end — also before an adjective (interminably long)

entries.meaning: Stopping and starting again at irregular intervals. ---
examples: It rained intermittently all afternoon.
The Wi-Fi has been working only intermittently.
She's worked intermittently as a substitute teacher.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Inside something, such as the body, a company or a country, rather than outside it. ---
examples: The job was advertised internally first.
He was bleeding internally after the crash.
The problem was handled internally, without calling the police.
entries.type: place — inside a body, organization or country
entries.position: end — also before a participle (internally generated)

entries.meaning: In or among many countries. ---
examples: She's an internationally famous architect.
The company now ships internationally.
His paintings have been shown internationally.
entries.русский: на международном уровне, по всему миру
entries.position: end — also before an adjective or participle (internationally known)

entries.meaning: Intimately has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She's intimately familiar with the city's history.
The two problems are intimately connected.
He knew the building intimately after working there for thirty years.
They talked intimately over a candlelit dinner.
Only a few people knew him intimately.

senses.head: In a very detailed or closely connected way
examples: She's intimately familiar with the city's history.
The two problems are intimately connected.
He knew the building intimately after working there for thirty years.

senses.head: In a close, personal or private way
examples: They talked intimately over a candlelit dinner.
Only a few people knew him intimately.

entries.position: before its word — for 'closely' (intimately familiar); end in the manner sense
entries.contrast: Intimately in intimately familiar or intimately connected is neutral and common; Russian интимно is narrower and suggests sex, which intimately does only in the context of relationships.

entries.meaning: So much that it is impossible to bear. ---
examples: The attic gets intolerably hot in July.
The noise from the construction site became intolerably loud.
The wait was intolerably long.
entries.position: before its word

entries.meaning: Into a muscle, usually by injection. ---
examples: The flu shot is given intramuscularly, usually in the upper arm.
The nurse injected the medicine intramuscularly.
This drug can be taken by mouth or intramuscularly.
entries.position: end
entries.form: -ly from intramuscular; in everyday speech often in the muscle

entries.meaning: Into a vein, usually through a needle or tube. ---
examples: The antibiotics were given intravenously.
She was so dehydrated they had to feed her intravenously.
The drug works faster when it's taken intravenously.
entries.position: end
entries.form: -ly from intravenous; in everyday speech often by IV

entries.meaning: With many small, complicated parts or details. ---
examples: The door was intricately carved with flowers.
The plot is intricately woven together.
Her dress was intricately embroidered by hand.
entries.position: before its word — usually a participle (intricately carved)

entries.meaning: Because of what something is in itself, not because of outside things. ---
examples: Gold isn't intrinsically valuable; people just agree that it is.
Is money intrinsically bad? I don't think so.
Learning is intrinsically rewarding for some students.
entries.type: degree — 'in itself, by nature', before an adjective
entries.position: before its word — usually an adjective (intrinsically valuable)
entries.form: -ally from intrinsic; the -al- is usually not pronounced

entries.meaning: By feeling rather than by reasoning, or in a way that is easy to understand without being taught. ---
examples: Intuitively, I felt I shouldn't trust him.
She seemed to understand intuitively what the baby wanted.
The new app is laid out more intuitively than the old one.
entries.position: any position — front with a comma; mid; before an adjective (intuitively obvious)

entries.meaning: Every time, without exception; always. ---
examples: The bus is invariably late on Mondays.
When I wash my car, it invariably rains the next day.
Her answers were invariably polite.
entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after be and the first auxiliary

entries.meaning: In a creative way that shows new ideas. ---
examples: The chef uses leftovers very inventively.
The old warehouse has been inventively turned into apartments.
The kids solved the puzzle more inventively than we expected.
entries.position: end — also before a participle

entries.meaning: In the opposite way, so that as one thing increases, the other decreases. ---
examples: Price and demand are often inversely related.
Speed is inversely proportional to the time a trip takes.
The strength of the signal varies inversely with the distance from the tower.
entries.position: before its word — usually related or proportional

entries.meaning: In a way that cannot be seen or noticed. ---
examples: The software updates run invisibly in the background.
The seam is invisibly stitched.
Mold can spread invisibly behind the walls.
entries.position: end — also mid

entries.meaning: In an attractive way that makes you want to come closer or try something. ---
examples: The pool sparkled invitingly in the sun.
She patted the seat next to her invitingly.
The smell of fresh bread drifted invitingly from the bakery.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Without meaning to or without being able to control it; also, against your will. ---
examples: I shivered involuntarily when the door creaked.
His leg jerked involuntarily.
About two hundred workers were laid off involuntarily.
entries.position: mid or end

entries.meaning: In your mind, without showing it to others. ---
examples: I smiled politely but inwardly groaned.
He looked calm but was inwardly panicking.
She was inwardly relieved when the meeting was canceled.
entries.type: manner — in the mind, not shown
entries.position: mid — often paired with outwardly (outwardly calm but inwardly furious)
entries.contrast: Inwardly is about hidden thoughts and feelings; for physical movement toward the inside, American English says inward (the door opens inward).

entries.meaning: In a very angry way. ---
examples: A customer called irately to complain about the bill.
"Where have you been?" she asked irately.
He waved his arms irately at the referee.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: Without good reason; not based on clear thinking. ---
examples: I know it's silly, but I'm irrationally afraid of elevators.
Investors often behave irrationally when markets fall.
He got irrationally angry over a parking spot.
entries.position: end — also before an adjective (irrationally afraid)

entries.meaning: Nonstandard for regardless: anyway, whatever happens. ---
examples: It might rain, but we're going irregardless.
Irregardless of what she says, I'm keeping the dog.
My uncle says irregardless all the time, and it drives my aunt crazy.
entries.русский: несмотря ни на что, в любом случае
entries.type: linking — a nonstandard form of regardless
entries.position: end — also with of before a noun
entries.contrast: Americans say irregardless often, but most teachers, editors and employers treat it as an error. Learn it to recognize it; in your own speech and writing use regardless.

entries.meaning: Irregularly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The newsletter comes out irregularly.
His heart was beating irregularly, so they ran more tests.
She eats irregularly when she's stressed.
The lot is irregularly shaped, which makes building difficult.
The stones were laid irregularly along the path.

senses.head: At uneven or unpredictable times, not on a regular schedule
examples: The newsletter comes out irregularly.
His heart was beating irregularly, so they ran more tests.
She eats irregularly when she's stressed.

senses.head: Not evenly or symmetrically shaped or arranged
examples: The lot is irregularly shaped, which makes building difficult.
The stones were laid irregularly along the path.

entries.type: frequency — at uneven times; also manner (irregularly shaped)
entries.position: end — for frequency; before its word before a participle (irregularly shaped)

entries.meaning: So badly that it cannot be fixed or made right. ---
examples: The painting was irreparably damaged in the flood.
Their friendship was irreparably harmed by the lie.
The scandal hurt his reputation irreparably.
entries.position: before its word — usually damaged or harmed; also end
entries.form: -ly from irreparable; stress on the second syllable, ih-REP-

entries.meaning: So strongly or attractively that you cannot resist. ---
examples: The puppy was irresistibly cute.
I was drawn irresistibly to the dessert table.
The song is irresistibly catchy.
entries.position: end — also before an adjective (irresistibly cute)

entries.meaning: Without thinking about the results of your actions. ---
examples: He spent the money irresponsibly.
The bank acted irresponsibly by lending to people who couldn't pay.
Teenagers sometimes drive irresponsibly.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: In a way that can never be recovered or put right. ---
examples: The files were irretrievably lost when the drive failed.
The court found that the marriage had broken down irretrievably.
Some trust, once broken, is irretrievably gone.
entries.position: before its word — usually lost or broken; also end

entries.meaning: Without the respect people usually expect, often in a funny way. ---
examples: The show pokes fun irreverently at politicians of both parties.
He spoke irreverently about the old traditions.
The book treats history irreverently but accurately.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: In a way that cannot be changed back. ---
examples: The climate may already be irreversibly changed.
Loud music can damage your hearing irreversibly.
Once you delete the account, your data is irreversibly erased.
entries.position: before its word — or end after a verb

entries.meaning: In a way that can never be changed or undone. ---
examples: The internet has irrevocably changed the way we shop.
After that night, their lives were irrevocably altered.
Once signed, the agreement binds you irrevocably.
entries.position: before its word — or end after a verb
entries.form: -ly from irrevocable; stress on the second syllable, ih-REV-

entries.meaning: In an annoyed, impatient way. ---
examples: "I heard you the first time," he said irritably.
She waved irritably at the flies.
He answered the phone irritably after the fifth call.
entries.position: end

entries.meaning: In a way that annoys you; also, used to say a fact is annoying.
examples: The website is irritatingly slow.
He's irritatingly cheerful first thing in the morning.
Irritatingly, the store closed five minutes before we got there.
entries.type: degree — before an adjective; also stance
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective (irritatingly slow); front with a comma as a stance adverb
